frase_gancho.texto: A reclining messenger holding the offering dish.

puente_narrativo.texto: After the offering dish, the smoke that went with it. Come closer to a brazier from Tula, made for burning copal and rubber in honor of the gods.

guion_corto.texto: This volcanic stone sculpture is a Chac Mool from Tula. A man lies on his back, with his knees bent and his elbows propped up, and turns his head ninety degrees to look at whoever approaches. On his belly he holds a circular dish where offerings were placed: copal, blood, perhaps hearts. He wears a butterfly pectoral, ear ornaments, and bracelets. He is not a god, but a messenger between people and the gods, placed at the entrance of temples. His name is neither Toltec nor Maya: it was given to him by a nineteenth-century explorer. And it is a type of sculpture that became famous in Tula and traveled all across Mexico.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at how he is positioned. His back is on the ground, his knees are bent, his elbows are propped up, and his head is suddenly turned to one side, as if someone had called him. On his belly there is a round dish. The posture is awkward, tense, and for that very reason unforgettable. He seems about to stand up, but he has been waiting for centuries.

His name is a curious story. In 1875, the explorer Augustus Le Plongeon found a sculpture like this one in Chichén Itzá and believed it was the portrait of a Maya king named Chaacmol, «red tiger». He was wrong about almost everything: it was not a king, and the name was made up. But it stuck. Today all sculptures of this type are called Chac Mool, even though we do not know what the people who made them called them.

What were they for? On the belly, the dish was a vessel for offerings: copal, branches, blood and, it is thought, hearts. In the Mexica tradition, a vessel like this was called cuauhxicalli, «gourd of the eagle». It should be understood as an altar and also as a kind of mailbox: whoever left an offering there was, in reality, sending it to the gods through the stone messenger.

Sculptures of this type stood at the doors of temples. In Tula, several have been found near the Palacio Quemado and Pyramid B. They have also been found in Chichén Itzá, in the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, and in several other regions. Today people debate where the idea was born: in Tula, in Chichén, or somewhere else. What is certain is that it was one of the most widely traveled images of ancient Mexico.

The Chac Mool from the Templo Mayor, by the way, is linked to the god of rain. It has features of Tláloc and stood right in the part of the temple that belonged to Tláloc. Thus, a type of sculpture that in Tula seems more closely tied to war becomes, among the Mexica, a figure for asking for water. It changed meaning without changing form. That happens a lot with images: they survive because they adapt.

A curious note. In 1954, the Mexican writer Carlos Fuentes published a story called «Chac Mool», in which one of these sculptures comes to life in a basement in Mexico City and little by little takes over its owner's house. It is one of the most famous fantasy stories in the country. Behind that story lies a very good intuition: these figures have something alive about them.

Look once more at the turning head. It is a very unusual gesture in ancient art, where almost everything looks straight ahead. Here, the messenger looks at you from the side, like someone watching over the entrance. It has been said that he symbolizes vigilance, or waiting. Perhaps it is simpler: whoever approaches the temple has to meet a gaze.

If you remember the skull of the [Disc of Death](mna_s04_disco_muerte), in the Teotihuacán Hall, or the Atlas figure that began this hall, you will see that Mesoamerican stone knows how to give movement to the motionless. This Chac Mool, tense and about to move, is a perfect example.

texto: Look at where the head turns and what kind of gaze it has
Notice the circular dish on the belly
Find the butterfly on the chest, the ear ornaments, and the bracelets

texto.Dimensions: 0.642 m high x 1.42 m long x 0.655 m thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: “Chac Mool” is the name the ancient people gave to this sculpture.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a modern name, from the nineteenth century; we do not know what the Toltec or the Maya called it.
